segments.text: Your sale records matter more than a headline rate.
segments.narration: Your sale records matter more than a headline rate.

For physical silver held as an investment, the long term collectibles rate can differ from the rates associated with stock gains. IRS guidance describes a maximum 28 percent rate for net collectibles gains. That does not mean every investor automatically pays 28 percent, and it is not a calculation of every tax that may apply. Some individuals may also face net investment income tax.

Your gain is based on what you actually realized from the sale minus your adjusted basis. Keep the purchase invoice, relevant acquisition costs, sale proceeds, and the dates connected with the particular items. A current spot price does not replace the amount you paid. If a record is missing or an amount is unclear, identify the question rather than filling it with a guess.

Under the general holding period rule, a gain is long term when the asset was held more than one year and short term when it was held one year or less. Special circumstances can affect the analysis. Explain gifts, inherited property, retirement accounts, or business holdings to a qualified tax professional before relying on a general investment sale overview.

Most capital asset sales are reported through Form 8949 and summarized on Schedule D. Use the instructions for the tax year of your sale. Do not confuse a dealer's information reporting threshold with your own filing obligation. A transaction can still belong on your return when no third party form arrives. Keep your own documents available to support the amounts reported.

Organize dates and identity, acquisition and basis evidence, and sale proceeds with their supporting documents. Connect the purchase invoice to the sale record and explain which items were sold if you disposed of only part of a holding. Keep fees identifiable so the person preparing the return can determine their appropriate treatment. Your worksheet should lead back to the underlying evidence.

This is a federal tax overview, not a determination of your state obligations or final liability. Check the edition of each IRS publication and the year covered by a rate table. Review the complete return with the relevant facts instead of multiplying a headline percentage by the sale proceeds. Use the article's primary sources and discuss unresolved questions with your preparer.
